analysis.one_liner: Cuts sulfur dioxide pollution from coal-fired power plants by 10 million tons, with federal subsidies for utilities.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a House vote: after six days of subcommittee hearings, its record folds it into H.R. 3030, the Clean Air Act rewrite that Congress passed later in the same session.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force a 10-million-ton nationwide cut in sulfur dioxide from coal- and oil-fired power plants over ten years, plus a 2-million-ton cut in nitrogen oxides. States would write compliance plans, governors of 13 high-emission states could certify their biggest plants instead, and a new federal fund — filled by a fee of up to 0.1 cents per kilowatt-hour on electricity — would reimburse utilities for up to 90% of the cost of installing scrubbers. It also barred utilities from using the new law to break coal supply contracts, protecting coal demand.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal plants, whose lakes, forests, and lungs bear the damage from acid rain and smog. Electric utilities also benefit, because a federal fund pays most of their compliance costs, and coal producers benefit because their supply contracts are shielded from termination.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a phased nationwide reduction of 10 million tons per year in sulfur dioxide from fossil-fuel power plants, measured from 1980 levels, over roughly ten years.
Directs EPA to set a 2-million-ton annual cap on nitrogen oxide emissions from power plants, the other main ingredient of acid rain and smog.
Requires states to publish cost and employment impact information for public comment before adopting final control plans, and requires utilities to make emissions records available to the public.
Makes energy conservation a priority and lets utilities substitute verified conservation savings for part of their required emissions cuts.
Requires that all subsidy payments from the new fund be 'for the benefit of the ratepayers' of the receiving utility.

analysis.who_pays: Electricity customers, through a fee of up to 0.1 cents per kilowatt-hour on fossil-fuel generation that utilities can pass along in rates, plus federal taxpayers, who fund the clean coal grant program and cover the capital costs of three federally contracted power plants.

drawbacks.text: The bill funds utility compliance through a fee on every kilowatt-hour generated, capped at 1.0 mill per kilowatt-hour through 2003 — a cost that falls on electricity customers, including people whose air is already clean.

It creates a federal 'Equity Fund' that reimburses utilities for up to 90% of the capital cost of scrubbers and up to 80% of clean coal technology, shifting costs from utility shareholders onto the Treasury and ratepayers.

It prohibits the early termination of existing coal supply contracts because of the law, deliberately preserving coal demand and coal mining jobs even where switching fuels would cut emissions faster.
Small utility plants can be exempted from emissions allocations where compliance costs would exceed the statewide average, leaving some polluting plants untouched.
The nitrogen oxide cap is conditional: EPA must set it by rule only if a study finds a net air quality benefit, adding a potential off-ramp.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The acid rain cuts are large and real, and the bill builds in public reporting, conservation incentives, and trading flexibility that could lower costs. But its design leans toward the regulated industries: utilities get most compliance costs paid from a fund financed by an electricity fee, coal supply contracts are protected from cancellation, and small plants can be excused. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this is one of the more industry-shielded ways to achieve a major pollution cut, and that the fee spreads costs to all ratepayers regardless of local air quality.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, whose subcommittees held six days of hearings on acid rain, and in May 1990 the record points the bill's further action to H.R. 3030 — the broader Clean Air Act Amendments that passed later that year and achieved the acid rain cuts without this bill's subsidy structure.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 17, 1989 and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
It was split between the Health and the Environment and Energy and Power subcommittees on July 31, 1989.
Those subcommittees held six days of hearings between September 7 and October 19, 1989.
The bill was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote in the House.
The final action entry, dated May 23, 1990, states 'For Further Action See H.R.3030', the bill that became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people lost little in the end, because the same Congress enacted the acid rain reductions through the successor Clean Air Act bill. Utilities and coal interests came out ahead, though: the final 1990 law used emissions allowance trading rather than this bill's taxpayer- and ratepayer-funded subsidies, and they had a full year of hearings to shape the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities and coal interests shaped the final law

for.name: Rep. Terry L. Bruce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through referral to two subcommittees that held hearings on it.

for.name: 3 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it small bipartisan support from the start.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees, held hearings through October 1989, and never reported H.R. 2909 to the full House; the committee's acid rain work instead went into the broader H.R. 3030.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 5 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors, all Illinois-area members — and the record shows no floor vote or roll call on which to judge a party split.

industries.note: They face mandatory sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide cuts, but a federal fund pays up to 90% of their capital costs and 80% of clean coal technology costs, financed by a kilowatt-hour fee passed to customers. Compliance costs are shifted off shareholders and onto ratepayers and taxpayers.

The bill's stated purpose includes keeping high- and low-sulfur coal miners employed, and it bans early termination of coal supply contracts triggered by the new rules, locking in coal demand even where fuel switching would cut emissions faster. Clean coal grants further channel public money toward continued coal use.

industries.industry: Scrubber and clean coal technology manufacturers
industries.note: Mandated emission cuts plus a federal grant program covering up to half the capital cost of new pollution-control technology create a large market for flue gas desulfurization and clean coal equipment.
